1. The image shows how much a typical stack of money, drawn as coin stacks next to a mortgage-rate line, compares across decades. It uses Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey data and an illustrative character, Tessa, standing by a house. It sets the 1991–1999 stack ($15,118) and the 2000s stack ($14,210) beside a 2010s stack ($20,374), when the rate was near 4.03%.

2. The coin stacks and decade labels are revealed one at a time. In frames 1–3 only the 1991–1999 and 2000s labels are shown, and a highlight sweeps along the rate line in frame 2. In frame 4 the 2010s stack and its label appear, along with a dashed line marking its height across the earlier stacks. Frames 5 and 6 hold that view. The orange bars and the blue rate line stay the same throughout.

3. It means that the "typical stack" figure was higher in the 2010s, a period of lower mortgage rates, than in the 1990s or 2000s. The chart labels it "illustrative" and says "US only · history, not a forecast." The image never says what the stack measures, so I can't say more about it than that.

4. A viewer wouldn't get a clear piece of advice from the image. At most, they might infer that the 2010s looked better than earlier decades, but nothing on screen says whether to pay down a mortgage early or invest instead.

5. The animation didn't suggest any advice. Its only on-screen guidance is the disclaimer "history, not a forecast," which discourages drawing a prediction from it. Anything beyond the comparison of decades would be my own conclusion.
